  audited feed model, workspace ingestion, Codex proxy/headless, ghosts/dedupe, debug bundles, scroll/layout, tests/
  docs, Claude-vs-Codex behavior, and deletion/reduction paths. I closed the orchestration run afterward.

  Core Diagnosis
  The recurring bug is not “the prompt is missing.” The prompt is usually present in state. The system keeps losing
  clarity because there are too many visual owners:

  - committed entries
  - semantic history
  - semantic current turn
  - work indicator
  - queued prompt strip
  - ghost fallback
  - debug-visible rows that only partially reflect the above

  PR #256 fixes the biggest transcript-ordering bug by moving committed entries, semantic history/current, work, and
  empty state into one ordered FeedRenderItem[]. That is the right direction.

  The recent “weird queued UI” happened because we over-applied that idea and treated pending input as if it belonged
  inside the scrollable transcript. It does not. The queue is composer-adjacent pending input, like upstream Codex/
  Claude. It should be modeled/debugged centrally, but physically rendered outside the scrollable feed.

  The Important Distinction
  We need one ownership/debug model, not necessarily one DOM container.

  Correct shape:

  PaneRenderModel {
    transcriptItems: FeedRenderItem[];   // scrollable Feed
    pendingInputItems: QueueItem[];      // fixed composer-adjacent QueueStrip
    footerSurfaces: readiness/conditions/toast/composer
    debugRows: all surfaces with exact placement/order/source
  }

  Wrong shape:

  FeedRenderItem[] includes queued-prompt

  That is what produced the ugly queued prompt row in the transcript.

  Why This Keeps Repeating
  Each prior fix solved one producer boundary but left another independent render surface alive.

  - Screen parsing was removed from assistant content, but committed/semantic/work/queue still had separate placement.
  - Semantic ownership got stricter, but provider-specific rules remained mixed into generic Feed.
  - Work indicator became cleaner, but became another row that needed ordering.
  - Ghost rendering became safer, but still exists as a fallback producer.
  - Codex optimistic prompt logic prevented duplicates, but used queuedMessages as a UI escape hatch.
  - Debug logs showed feed rows but not all visible surfaces, so queue bugs looked like “missing prompt” until the
    manual HTML bundle exposed it.

  What PR #256 Does Right
  Keep this:

  - deriveFeedRenderModel() returning an ordered items list.
  - Feed rendering via renderItems.map(...).
  - Semantic history/current/work participating in the same transcript ordering.
  - Tests for stale semantic history appearing before newer prompts.
  - Queue restored outside Feed in QueueStrip.

  That directly fixes the “prompt exists but is buried under stale semantic history/work” class.

  Still Fragile
  The agents found several real risks:

  - shouldQueueOptimisticCodexUserEntry() still queues based partly on semantic-history renderability. With unified
    ordering, semantic history no longer proves the prompt must be queued.
  - Semantic timestamps are receipt-time-ish in places; late semantic events can still sort oddly versus committed
    entries.
  - renderModel.ts decides a semantic item is renderable, but renderUnits.ts / StreamingTurn.tsx can later suppress all
    units. That means selector and component can disagree.
  - FeedRenderModel still exposes compatibility fields like visibleEntries, renderedSemanticHistory,
    renderedSemanticTurn, shouldShowWorkIndicator.
  - Queue is visually correct as a sibling, but is not represented strongly enough in debug/visible row output.
  - Claude provider queues are provider-authored JSONL queue-operations; Codex queues are local optimistic UI
    placeholders. They share queuedMessages, which hides a major semantic difference.
  - Codex gets normalized into Claude-shaped Entry objects, including tool results as user-role blocks. That leaks
    provider semantics into generic Feed.

  What Can Go
  Eventually safe to delete after replacement:

  - legacy FeedRenderModel compatibility buckets
  - old Feed bucket render paths
  - special empty branch once empty renders through item renderer
  - vague debug slot values once exact item/surface debug rows exist
  - production fallback tool-index rebuilding in Feed
  - stale docs/comments saying queued prompts are “feed items”
  - duplicate Todo rendering components after extracting one presentational component

  Do not delete yet:

  - QueueStrip
  - shouldQueueOptimisticCodexUserEntry()
  - semantic committed-text suppression
  - ghost fallback predicates
  - Codex-to-Entry compatibility mapping
  - JSONL coalescing
  - WorkIndicator

  Those are ugly, but they are still protecting real edge cases.

  Recommended Next Fix
  I would not do a giant rewrite first. I’d do one hardening PR after #256:

  1. Rename the concept clearly: queue is pendingInput, not feed item.
  2. Add a pane-level render/debug model that includes both transcriptItems and pendingInputItems.
  3. Keep QueueStrip outside Feed, but make debug bundles log it with key, timestamp, text hash/snippet, provider,
     placement, and reconciliation status.
  4. Remove semantic-history from the Codex queue predicate, or at least gate it behind a test proving it is still
     needed after unified ordering.
  5. Make semantic renderability single-source: model should carry render units or a renderability result that UI cannot
     silently invalidate.
  6. Use upstream semantic event timestamps/sequence where available instead of mixed local Date.now() ordering.
  7. Add DOM/layout regression asserting queued prompt is outside the feed scroller and between Feed and composer.
  8. Update stale docs in feed-render-item-plan.md so nobody re-adds queued prompts into Feed.

  Test Matrix We Need
  Add focused simulation tests, not huge E2E first:

  - late semantic history arrives after a user prompt, but renders before it chronologically
  - same-millisecond semantic/user timestamp tie
  - missing timestamp on committed user prompt
  - Codex submit during active current turn
  - Codex submit after semantic history exists but no live current turn
  - queued prompt reconciles when rollout user row arrives
  - failed send rolls back optimistic/awaiting state
  - queue strip DOM is outside feed scroller
  - debug bundle includes queue surface even though it is not a feed row
  - Claude provider queue-operation and Codex local queue are distinguishable

  Bottom line: PR #256 is worth keeping. The next architectural move is not “put every visible thing into Feed.” It is
  “make one pane render model own every visible surface, while Feed remains only the scrollable transcript.”

That's issue #248 — "Tiled Dispatch" (no labels, no comments yet). Here's what it's about.

The problem it solves

Dispatch Mode today is a single command-center surface: you see the list of all your agents, pick one, and work with
it. That's serial. When you're coordinating 5+ Claude/Codex agents, you want two things at once that the current
design can't give you:

1. A full index of every agent (worktrees, section titles, provider labels, full titles).
2. Several live agent views side-by-side, each independently switchable.

The proposed feature

A new command, Tiled Dispatch, that prompts: "How many dispatch tiles? 1–10". Enter N and you get a multi-lane layout:

[full dispatch index] [agent view 1] [mini list 2] [agent view 2] … [mini list N] [agent view N]

- Lane 1 is special — it keeps the full Dispatch list: section titles, worktree/project grouping, provider/type
labels. It's the global index for the whole layout.
- Every later lane gets a compact mini-list (no repeated section titles/worktrees/labels — just enough to switch that
lane) plus its own live agent view beside it.
- Each lane shows a different live agent, and they're independent — switching one lane doesn't steal focus or
selection from another.

The clever bit — scroll vs. selection decoupling

This is the subtle design point. When you scroll a mini-list (say lane 3), the full left index follows that scroll
position so you keep rich context for the region you're browsing — but the left index's highlight stays on lane 1's
selected agent. So scrolling lane 3 moves the index's viewport without making it pretend lane 3's agent is "selected."
Scroll-sync and selection-highlight are deliberately separate concerns.

Key constraints (acceptance criteria worth flagging)

- Count clamped to 1–10; default conservative (2).
- Same agent process/session is reused — switching tiled views must not respawn agents.
- Exiting tiled Dispatch must not kill agents — returns to normal workspace.
- Needs horizontal overflow / responsive compression for high tile counts.

Open questions still unresolved

- Persist across app reloads, or transient view mode?
- Should each lane remember its agent by session id across exits?
- Resizable lane widths? Pinned/sticky full-index lane while right lanes scroll horizontally?
- Preserve lane selections when tile count changes?

In short: it turns Dispatch from a one-agent-at-a-time command center into a tiled, multi-lane cockpit — one rich
master index on the left, plus N independently-controllable live agent panes, with scroll-context sync that doesn't
clobber per-lane selection. It directly serves the project's "run 5+ agents at once" thesis.

Note: this is the only issue about viewing multiple Dispatch lanes at once. (#236 and #261 are related Dispatch bugs —
focus-stealing and focus-on-close — but #248 is the multi-lane feature itself.)

I've read the whole thing — it's a compact single-file project. Here's a full walkthrough.

What it is

A Discord bot that watches hackathon listing APIs and auto-posts new hackathons into a Discord channel as rich embeds.
Node 20+, ESM, one runtime dependency (discord.js v14). All logic lives in src/index.js (~550 lines).

How it runs

- npm start → node --env-file=.env src/index.js (config comes entirely from env vars).
- main() requires DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN, DISCORD_CHANNEL_ID, and at least one hackathon API URL, logs into Discord, and on
the clientReady event runs one poll immediately, then repeats every POLL_INTERVAL_MINUTES (default 60, floored at 5)
via setInterval.
- Intents are minimal (Guilds only) — it only sends messages, never reads them.

The poll cycle (pollAndPost, line 436)

1. Fetch each configured API URL (fetchHackathons, line 413). Sends Accept: application/json, optional Authorization
from API_AUTH_HEADER. Validates HTTP status and that the content-type is JSON (otherwise throws with a body snippet).
One failing source is logged and skipped, not fatal.
2. Extract events from arbitrary JSON shapes (extractEvents, line 314): prefers a data: [...] envelope, otherwise
recursively walks the payload (collectArrays) and picks the largest array of objects, otherwise treats the root as an
array.
3. Normalize each item (normalizeItem, line 228) into a uniform shape by trying many possible key names for
id/title/url/location/start/end/description/topics. It's defensively written to handle several different API schemas.
Descriptions are truncated to ~400 chars, topics to ~500.
4. Merge + dedupe across sources (mergeDedupeEvents, line 83) by id and by a normalized URL (normalizedEventUrl strips
hash, sorts query params, lowercases) so the same hackathon listed on two backends isn't posted twice. First
occurrence wins, ordered by your env URL list.
5. Filter to new events using a persisted "seen" set, then post each as an embed, oldest-first, and save the seen set.

State / persistence

- data/seen-hackathons.json stores { ids: [...], updatedAt }. loadSeen/saveSeen (lines 342–359) track which hackathon
IDs have already been posted, so restarts don't re-spam. The data/ dir is gitignored.

Notable behavior flags (env-driven)

- SKIP_INITIAL_POST — on a fresh run (empty seen set), record all current hackathons as "seen" without posting, so you
don't dump the entire backlog on first launch.
- FORCE_POST — re-post everything once on the first poll (re-seeding), then reverts to normal. Guarded so it doesn't
spam every interval (line 516).
- POLL_INTERVAL_MINUTES, HACKATHON_API_URL (single) / HACKATHON_API_URLS (comma/newline list), API_AUTH_HEADER.

Signup link logic (signupUrlForEvent, line 33)

Picks the "Sign up" link per source:
- HackTrack/EU source → uses the event's own url (e.g. lu.ma), falling back to HACKTRACK_SIGNUP_URL / a hardcoded
Vercel site.
- Builderbase source → prefers SIGNUP_PAGE_URL, then a discovery default, then the event URL.
- Otherwise → event URL or SIGNUP_PAGE_URL.

Embeds (buildEmbed, line 371)

Discord embed with title, URL, description, a "Details" field (start/end formatted via toLocaleString, a
human-readable duration from formatDurationBetween, location, topics), Discord blurple color, a timestamp from the
event start/end, and a "Sign up" link field. All fields respect Discord's length limits (1024 for fields).

Quick observations

- Solid defensive design for unknown/varied API schemas, and graceful per-source failure handling.
- seen grows unbounded — IDs are never pruned, so seen-hackathons.json only ever grows. Fine in practice for this
volume.
- No data/ dir committed, created on demand by saveSeen. There's no .env.example or README, so the env-var contract is
only discoverable by reading the code (which is what I just did).
- Uses the newer clientReady event name (discord.js v14.16+), so the pinned ^14.16.3 matters.

How it works

One row per concept, source_lang="en", source=<english master>, translations_json={en, sv, de, …}, plus approved =

Reading (translation time):
- For any pair (e.g. sv→de), look up the master row that contains the source-language form → return the

- The AI already emits the term + variations; we add glossary_master_en = the canonical English form (generated even

**BLOCKER — AppRunJournal.ts:162 + 410-412 (index.ts) — the final flush on quit is lost; last events never reach disk.**
`stop()` does `void this.flush()` — fire-and-forget async. The `will-quit` handler (index.ts:409-415) is synchronous and never calls `event.preventDefault()`, so Electron tears the process down on the same tick. The `flush()` promise chain (`mkdir` + async `writeFile`) cannot resolve before exit, so the `app.will_quit` event recorded at index.ts:410 — plus **everything still in `pending`** — is dropped on every clean shutdown. This directly defeats invariant #3 ("the last events.jsonl append lands before exit"). Worse, this is the *normal* path, not an edge case.
*Fix:* In `stop()`, drain `pending` synchronously with `appendFileSync` (mirror `markCleanShutdown`), or have `markCleanShutdown` sync-append the whole pending batch (not just the clean-shutdown event) before writing the marker.

**MAJOR — AppRunJournal.ts:135-154 — write failure silently discards the batch; events are lost, not retried.**
`takePendingBatch()` (line 137) removes events from `pending` *before* the write is attempted. If the `writeFile(..., flag:'a')` rejects (line 144), the `.catch` at 146 logs and swallows — the batch is gone forever and is never re-queued. So a transient disk error doesn't cost "old breadcrumbs" (the stated drop-oldest tradeoff); it costs the *most recent* events with no counter and no record that they were lost. The `events_dropped` accounting (line 199-208) only covers cap-overflow drops, not write-failure drops.
*Why it matters:* During exactly the unhealthy-disk scenario the journal exists to explain, you lose the newest evidence with zero trace.
*Fix:* On write rejection, either re-`unshift` the batch back onto `pending` (bounded by the cap) or increment a distinct `failedWriteEvents` counter that surfaces in the next heartbeat/event.

**MAJOR — AppRunJournal.ts:140-145 — non-atomic mkdir+append inside the writeQueue is a misuse of "serialized" and can corrupt a line on partial write.** `writeFile(path, lines, {flag:'a'})` opens, writes, and closes per call. For multi-KB batches a single `write(2)` is not guaranteed atomic, and there is no `fsync`. Combined with the swallowed-rejection path above, a mid-write failure can leave a truncated (invalid-JSON) trailing line in `events.jsonl`, which a strict JSONL reader will choke on. The serialization via `writeQueue` prevents *interleaving between batches* but does nothing about *intra-batch* torn writes.

**MINOR — AppRunJournal.ts:140-141 — `.catch(()=>{})` on the *previous* link hides nothing harmful here, but the chain grows unbounded.** Each `flush()` reassigns `this.writeQueue = this.writeQueue.catch().then().catch()`. However the promise chain is never reset to `Promise.resolve()`, so over a long-lived run it accumulates a long resolved-promise chain. Agent Code is an open-source Electron IDE for running many real coding agents—primarily Claude Code and Codex—inside a tiled, persistent workspace. It is not a thin model API client and does not recreate the providers’ agent loops.

OpenCode support also exists, although it is less complete: fresh sessions work through opencode serve, but offline session listing and file-based transcript resolution are still missing.

Why it exists
The project rejects two common compromises:

Provider SDKs expose only a subset of what the real CLIs can do.
Third-party clients risk losing provider authentication access and generally cannot preserve native CLI behavior.
Agent Code instead acts as a “middleman” around installed binaries. This provides:

Many simultaneous agents in tiled grids or Dispatch.
Persistent tmux-backed terminals.
Custom React rendering of transcripts, tools, git commands, permissions, and streaming output.
Session switching between Claude and Codex.

How it works
The main runtime path is:

React renderer
    ⇅ typed IPC through preload
Electron main / SessionManager
    ⇅ provider registry
ClaudeSession / CodexSession / OpencodeSession
    ⇅
real CLI in PTY, or OpenCode HTTP/SSE
    ⇅
semantic + screen + committed transcript channels
    ⇅
custom provider-aware React feed
Important boundaries:

The renderer owns tabs, panes, grids, Dispatch, workspace layout, and UI state. Main intentionally does not know what a pane or split is.
Electron main owns processes, PTYs, transcript watchers, persistence, tmux recovery, MCP hosts, diagnostics, and IPC.
The preload bridge exposes a large typed, domain-split API; renderer code does not access Node directly.
claude-code-headless and codex-headless run the actual installed CLIs in PTYs and combine terminal mirrors, native transcript tailing, screen parsers, and optional proxy streaming.
opencode-headless is intentionally an HTTP/SSE adapter, not a PTY wrapper.

Path	Purpose
